In Adobe Experience Platform, identity keys are unique identifiers like ECID, Email, Phone, or Loyalty ID that link data across systems. These are stored in namespaces and used for identity stitching, profile merging, and privacy lookups.Profile attributes, on the other hand, are descriptive values such as firstName, city, or loyaltyTier. They help enrich a profile but do not participate in matching or resolution unless explicitly set as identities.To summarise: Identity Key Examples:ECID (Experience Cloud ID)EmailPhone numberGAID (Google Advertising ID)IDFA (Apple Identifier for Advertisers)TNTID (Adobe Target ID)CRM IDLoyalty IDSubscriber IDLogin UsernameWeb Account IDDevice IDDeclared ID (custom)❌ Profile Attribute Examples:firstName, lastNamegender, age, dateOfBirthcity, region, countryloyaltyTier, membershipLevelpreferredLanguage, accountStatuslastPurchaseDate, totalSpendoptInStatus, lastLoginDateIdentity keys define who the person is, while attributes describe what we know about them.

A flattened join in Adobe Experience Platform (AEP) refers to a simplified, one-directional relationship between two datasets.— typically from an XDM Profile or Experience Event dataset to a lookup table.Unlike relational databases, AEP does not support dynamic or many-to-many joins. Instead, data from the lookup table is merged into the referencing record at runtime based on a single key.Flattened joins are used in AEP to ensure compatibility with its underlying Parquet-based columnar storage, which is optimised for fast reads of denormalised data. Parquet performs best when data is wide and flat, not deeply nested or relational. Flattening lookups at runtime allows AEP to maintain high performance across identity stitching, segmentation, and activation, especially at scale and in edge scenarios where low latency is critical.This model supports only one-to-one or many-to-one relationships. The primary dataset (e.g. a profile) must reference exactly one row in the lookup dataset. That row's values are then “flattened” into the profile during evaluation. This avoids relational complexity and supports fast, scalable profile stitching and segmentation.Examples:Profile Dataset Lookup Dataset------------------ ---------------------userId: 123 tierId: goldname: Alice ---> discount: 10%tierId: gold tierLabel: Gold TieruserId: 123name: AlicetierId: golddiscount: 10%tierLabel: Gold Tier

Correct standard namespaces for browsing profiles in AEP include:GAID (Google Advertising ID)PhoneTNTID (Adobe Target ID)Declared ID is a common namespace, but it’s not directly browsable in the profile UI. It's typically used for identity stitching via ingestion, not for direct lookups.Similarly, Address isn’t a namespace at all — it’s a profile attribute.When using the Profile Viewer in AEP, only specific standard namespaces are enabled for profile lookup, and these vary slightly based on license and setup. The key is: browseable ≠ all available.Each identity in AEP must be associated with a namespace to participate in profile stitching, segment qualification, or personalisation. Adobe provides both standard namespaces (like Email, GAID, ECID, TNTID) and allows for the creation of custom namespaces (like CRM ID, Declared ID, Loyalty ID).Namespaces power the Identity Graph by letting AEP know which identities belong to the same person. For example, if a profile has both ECID: abc123 and Email: jsmith@example.com, the namespace tells AEP these are different types of IDs — and can be stitched together if linked by data ingestion.

When a segment is created for streaming or edge evaluation in Adobe Experience Platform, qualifying profiles will not be added instantly. Adobe guarantees inclusion within the next 24 hours.Streaming and edge segments are designed for near real-time responsiveness, but not all profiles qualify the moment the segment is saved. This is because profiles are evaluated as new data flows into the system, and Adobe allows time for processing across regions and services.As a best practice, segment-driven activations or journeys should be designed with this latency in mind. Avoid triggering downstream actions under the assumption that all eligible profiles will be present immediately after segment creation.If it is new, it takes time to sort itself out.

Konductor is Adobe’s internal name for the orchestration engine that powers the Unified Edge. GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) is a comprehensive data privacy law enforced by the European Union that governs how organisations collect, store, process, and share personal data of individuals in the EU. It emphasises user consent, data transparency, and the right to access or delete one’s data. Example: Under GDPR, a company must obtain explicit consent before using someone’s email for marketing. If the user withdraws consent, the company is obligated to stop processing and remove that data upon request.

DULE (Data Usage Labeling and Enforcement) is a governance framework in Adobe Experience Platform that allows organisations to label data (e.g. PII, sensitive, region-specific) and enforce policies that control how that data can be used or activated. It ensures compliance by automatically blocking actions that violate defined usage rules. Example: If email addresses are labeled as pii, and a policy prohibits activating pii data to third-party destinations like Facebook, AEP will automatically block such an export to ensure data compliance.
